moments.title: Traditional date of first Ancient Olympics
moments.body:
Ancient Greek sources record stadion races at Olympia continuing into the late Roman period.

The Games are abolished around 393 CE under Theodosius I.
moments.takeaway: Athletic competition existed as a religious and civic institution long before modern sport.

moments.title: First modern Olympics
moments.body:
Approximately 240 male athletes from 14 nations compete in 43 events.

Women first compete in tennis and golf at Paris 1900.
moments.takeaway: The modern Games revived a tradition while adding new institutional structures.

moments.title: First Paralympic Games
moments.body: Building on Guttmann's 1948 Stoke Mandeville games for spinal-injured veterans, the first official Paralympics are held in Rome with 400 athletes from 23 nations.
moments.takeaway: Para-sport began as rehabilitative medicine and grew into a major international movement.

now.title: The Olympic movement today
now.body: Recent Games involve over 10,000 athletes. Cost overruns, doping scandals and disputes over participation policies dominate governance debates.
now.open_questions: How should cost and environmental impact be weighed against the cultural value of hosting? How should categories be defined for elite competition?

items.reflection: The modern Olympics often present themselves as direct heirs of antiquity, but the institutional gap is huge and the reinvention is recent.

moments.title: Title IX signed
moments.body: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programmes, including athletics.
moments.takeaway: A general civil rights law had outsized effects on sport participation.

moments.title: First Women's World Cup
moments.body:
Twelve teams compete in Guangdong; the United States wins.

Women's football grows steadily in subsequent decades, alongside ongoing debates over pay and investment.
moments.takeaway: International women's competitions consolidated after national-level shifts.

moments.title: Every Olympic nation includes women
moments.body: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Brunei send female athletes for the first time, meaning every participating nation has female athletes.
moments.takeaway: Institutional integration of women athletes was achieved at the world level only in the 21st century.

now.title: Sport participation today
now.body: Female participation has risen sharply since the 1970s, alongside continuing gaps in pay, coverage and facility access. Questions of eligibility in women's competition are politically and scientifically contested.
now.open_questions: How should world federations balance fairness, inclusion and safety in eligibility policies?

items.reflection: Sport policy is one of the clearest examples of how legal frameworks reshape participation across a single generation.

moments.title: Hill and Lupton on oxygen uptake
moments.body: Hill (Nobel laureate 1922) and Lupton describe maximal oxygen uptake as a determinant of endurance performance.
moments.takeaway: Modern sport science began in physiology labs working on energy metabolism.

moments.title: Saltin and Astrand on training
moments.body: Scandinavian research establishes detailed relationships between training, cardiac output and endurance.
moments.takeaway: Cross-national research consortia produced the modern training evidence base.

moments.title: 'Live high, train low' published
moments.body: Their study supports a protocol where athletes live at altitude but train at lower elevations, balancing adaptation and intensity.
moments.takeaway: Elite-level training innovations often emerge from carefully controlled physiological studies.

now.title: Sport science today
now.body: Wearable sensors and biomechanics labs allow individualised monitoring. Open questions remain about overtraining markers and long-term injury risk.
now.open_questions: How well do laboratory measures predict competitive performance? What ethical limits apply to performance technologies short of doping?

items.reflection: Sport science walks a line between performance enhancement, athlete welfare and the integrity of competition.

moments.title: IOC founded at the Sorbonne
moments.body: On 23 June 1894, Coubertin convenes the International Athletic Congress at the Sorbonne. Delegates from 9 countries agree to revive the Olympic Games. The International Olympic Committee is formed. Coubertin, inspired by Thomas Arnold's Rugby School and the Wenlock Olympian Games (Shropshire, since 1850), saw sport as moral education.
moments.takeaway: The modern Olympic movement was created by a French aristocrat inspired by English public-school muscular Christianity.

moments.title: Jesse Owens at Berlin
moments.body: African American sprinter Jesse Owens wins four gold medals (100m, 200m, long jump, 4x100m relay) at the Nazi-hosted Berlin Olympics. Hitler had hoped the Games would demonstrate Aryan supremacy. Owens befriends German long jumper Luz Long, who advised him on his approach run after a foul. Owens was famously not snubbed by Hitler — but was largely ignored by President Roosevelt back home.

quote.text: Hitler didn't snub me — it was [our president] who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram.

moments.takeaway: An African American athlete demolished Nazi racial ideology in front of Hitler, then returned to a segregated America.

now.title: Olympic movement today
now.body: The IOC governs the Summer and Winter Olympics, with revenues over $7bn per 4-year cycle. Recent Games (Tokyo 2020, Beijing 2022, Paris 2024) have grappled with cost, climate, and athlete welfare. The 'Olympic Truce' is regularly invoked; geopolitical tensions (Russia, Israel) increasingly test it.
now.open_questions: How can the Games be hosted without bankrupting cities? LA 2028 and Brisbane 2032 use mostly existing venues.

items.reflection: Coubertin's vision was explicitly elitist and male-only ('The Olympic Games... with the solemn and periodic exaltation of male athleticism, with internationalism as a base...'). Every later opening of the Games to women, Black athletes, professionals and Para-athletes was a fight against his founding intent.

moments.title: Black power salute on the podium
moments.who: Tommie Smith, John Carlos, Peter Norman
moments.body: On 16 October 1968 in Mexico City, after Smith wins the 200m gold (in a then world-record 19.83s) and Carlos bronze, both Americans raise gloved fists during the national anthem. Australian silver medallist Peter Norman wears an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge in solidarity. Smith and Carlos are immediately expelled from the Olympic Village.

quote.text: If I win I am an American, not a black American. But if I did something bad, then they would say 'a Negro'. We are black and we are proud of being black.

moments.takeaway: A 50-second podium moment in 1968 reshaped how sport relates to political protest. Smith, Carlos and Norman all paid significant career costs.

now.title: Athlete protest today
now.body: Colin Kaepernick's NFL kneeling (2016), Megan Rapinoe, women's football, and Black Lives Matter activism extend the lineage. Tokyo 2020 allowed limited protest gestures (kneeling, raised fists at certain moments). Saudi-funded sport and athlete welfare conflicts are the current frontier.
now.open_questions: How do athletes navigate sponsor contracts, federation rules and platform incentives in expressing political views?

items.reflection: Peter Norman never ran another Olympics for Australia despite qualifying. When he died in 2006, Smith and Carlos were pallbearers at his funeral. Olympic Project for Human Rights badges remain rare; allyship at personal cost is rarer.

moments.title: Munich massacre
moments.body: On 5 September 1972, Palestinian Black September militants take 11 Israeli athletes and coaches hostage at the Olympic Village. A botched rescue at Fürstenfeldbruck airbase leaves all 11 Israelis, 5 attackers and 1 German police officer dead. IOC President Avery Brundage announces 'The Games must go on' after a 34-hour suspension.
moments.takeaway: The Games' continuation after Munich set a controversial precedent about how international sport responds to terrorism.

now.title: Olympic security today
now.body: Olympic security budgets are now in the billions (Paris 2024: ~€320m for security alone; London 2012: £553m). The IOC formally commemorated the Munich victims for the first time at Tokyo 2020 — 49 years later. Israel was the first delegation to honour them officially each Games.
now.open_questions: How do mega-events balance openness with security in an era of terrorism, cybersecurity threats and disinformation?

items.reflection: The widow of fencing coach Andre Spitzer campaigned for decades for IOC commemoration. Institutional acknowledgement of loss often takes longer than the lives lost.

moments.title: Stoke Mandeville Games
moments.body: Ludwig Guttmann, a Jewish neurologist who had fled Nazi Germany in 1939, runs the Spinal Injuries Centre at Stoke Mandeville Hospital. On 29 July 1948 — the day of the London Olympics opening ceremony — he organises an archery competition for 16 patients (including 2 women), all WWII servicemen and women with spinal injuries.
moments.takeaway: Para-sport was founded by a refugee neurologist as therapy, on the same day as the Olympics he could not compete in.

moments.title: Beijing Paralympics scale up
moments.body: Beijing 2008 marks a step-change in Paralympic broadcasting and participation: 3,951 athletes from 146 countries. The IPC, founded in 1989, has equal IOC partnership. London 2012 sells out almost every Paralympic event for the first time; Channel 4's coverage transforms perception in the UK.
moments.takeaway: Within 60 years, an archery competition for 16 patients became a global mega-event with thousands of elite athletes.

now.title: Para-sport today
now.body: Paris 2024 featured 4,400 Para-athletes from 168 nations. Classification systems (defining functional categories) remain contested and complex. Para-athletes like Tanni Grey-Thompson (UK, 11 Paralympic golds), Ellie Simmonds (UK, swimming), David Weir (UK, wheelchair racing) and Trischa Zorn (US, swimming, 55 medals) have public profiles unimaginable a generation ago.
now.open_questions: How can Para-athletes earn proportionate to Olympic counterparts? Prize money, sponsorship and broadcasting gaps persist.

items.reflection: Guttmann was 50 when he ran the first games. He won a knighthood (1966) and a posthumous reputation as 'father of the Paralympics'. The man Nazi Germany expelled built one of Britain's most enduring sporting contributions.

moments.title: Roger Bannister breaks 4 minutes
moments.body: On 6 May 1954 at Iffley Road track, Oxford, medical student Bannister runs a mile in 3:59.4, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. The crowd of 3,000 hears the first announcement break off after 'three' — Norris McWhirter's deliberate pause to maximise drama. 46 days later, Australian John Landy lowers the record to 3:58.0.

quote.attrib: Norris McWhirter announcing Bannister's time, 6 May 1954

moments.takeaway: Bannister was a part-time runner with a hospital job. The 'impossible' record was broken by an amateur preparing in lunch breaks.

moments.title: Usain Bolt's 9.58s 100m
moments.body: On 16 August 2009 Bolt runs the 100m in 9.58 seconds — the largest single-race improvement in 30 years (0.11s off his own world record). His top speed exceeds 44 km/h. The record still stands.
moments.takeaway: Athletics records typically fall by hundredths; Bolt rewrote sprinting by tenths. Genetic variation, training, technology and stadium conditions all combined.

now.title: Athletics today
now.body: World Athletics (formerly IAAF) governs the sport. Eliud Kipchoge's sub-2-hour marathon (1:59:40, Vienna 2019, unofficial) was the 4-minute-mile equivalent of its era — assisted by pacers and shoe technology. Nike Vaporfly and successor shoes triggered controversies and rule changes (40mm sole limit).
now.open_questions: How should performance-enhancing technology be regulated? The line between innovation and unfair advantage moves over time.

items.reflection: Bannister became a neurologist and dismissed his mile as far less important than his medical work. The athlete he was for one afternoon overshadowed the doctor he was for 50 years.

moments.title: Battle of the Sexes
moments.who: Billie Jean King vs Bobby Riggs, Houston Astrodome
moments.body: On 20 September 1973, 29-year-old Billie Jean King defeats 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 in front of 30,492 spectators (still a US tennis record) and an estimated 90 million TV viewers. Riggs had defeated Margaret Court 6-2 6-1 earlier in 1973. King later said: 'I thought it would set us back 50 years if I didn't win that match.'
moments.takeaway: A single tennis match watched by 90 million people shifted attitudes about women's sport in a way no policy could match.

now.title: Women's tennis today
now.body: King founded the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) in 1973. Prize money parity reached Wimbledon (2007), with Venus Williams a leading voice. The WTA's 2021 stand against China after the Peng Shuai disappearance was a rare modern example of a sport governing body confronting a major state.
now.open_questions: Why has tennis achieved prize-money parity at majors while most other sports have not?

items.reflection: King also founded the Women's Sports Foundation (1974) and was the first openly lesbian top-tier athlete (outed in 1981; she lost endorsements estimated at $2 million). Her 2014 USTA recognition came decades late.

moments.title: Women's 800m run at the Olympics
moments.body: Women run the 800m at the Olympics for the first and only time until 1960. Lina Radke (Germany) wins in 2:16.8 — a world record that stands for 16 years. Reports — largely fictionalised — claim several women collapse exhausted. The IOC bars women from races longer than 200m for 32 years.
moments.takeaway: Misogynist mythology about women's physical 'fragility' kept the women's 800m out of the Olympics for over three decades. Most contemporary medical opinion agreed; the photos disagreed.

now.title: Women's athletics today
now.body: Women run every event men do, often closer to men's times than is widely understood (e.g. 10% gap in marathons). The women's marathon was added to the Olympics in 1984 (Joan Benoit won). The 2024 Paris Olympics had exactly equal numbers of male and female athletes for the first time in history.
now.open_questions: Why are participation gaps in elite sport closing faster than in coaching, officiating and governance?

items.reflection: Bobbi Gibb ran the Boston Marathon disguised as a man in 1966. Kathrine Switzer registered with initials in 1967 and was physically attacked by race director Jock Semple. The marathon was 'too dangerous' for women for years after Frank Shorter won Olympic gold in 1972.

moments.title: Football Association founded
moments.body: On 26 October 1863 at the Freemasons' Tavern in London, representatives of 12 clubs meet and codify rules for 'association football'. The Cambridge Rules (1848, written at Trinity College Cambridge) and Sheffield Rules (1858) had attempted earlier codifications. Rugby football, which permitted carrying the ball, split off after this meeting.
moments.takeaway: Modern football emerged from a series of attempts to standardise rules that public-school boys could play against each other. Association vs Rugby is a 19th-century English schism.

moments.title: First FIFA World Cup
moments.body: 13 teams compete in Montevideo, July 1930. European nations are reluctant to travel; only 4 turn up. Uruguay (defending Olympic champions) win 4-2 in the final against Argentina. The trophy — later the Jules Rimet Cup — was hidden in a shoebox during WWII.
moments.takeaway: The first World Cup was a Latin American affair; European football's global dominance came later.

moments.title: Hillsborough disaster
moments.body: On 15 April 1989, 97 Liverpool supporters die in a crush at the Leppings Lane terrace at Hillsborough Stadium during the FA Cup semi-final. The Taylor Report (1990) recommends all-seater stadia for top-flight football. The Sun's false reporting (cleared up only in 2016 inquest verdict of unlawful killing) damaged its Liverpool sales for decades.
moments.takeaway: 97 deaths drove a transformation of English football grounds. The truth — that police failure, not fans, caused the deaths — took 27 years to be formally acknowledged.

now.title: Football today
now.body: The English Premier League (founded 1992) has revenue over £6bn/season. The 2022 men's World Cup (Qatar) involved >6,000 reported migrant worker deaths in construction and other industries. Women's football has grown rapidly (Lionesses winning Euro 2022, 87,192 attendance at Wembley final).
now.open_questions: How can football's governance reckon with state-ownership, sportswashing and human-rights concerns at host nations?

items.reflection: Football's global reach is unparalleled in sport. The cost of that scale includes Heysel (1985, 39 deaths), Hillsborough (1989), and modern tragedies (Indonesia's Kanjuruhan 2022, 135 deaths). Crowd safety is policy, not nature.

moments.title: First Wimbledon
moments.who: All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club
moments.body: The first Wimbledon Championships are held in July 1877: 22 men compete on grass courts. Spencer Gore wins. The tournament was created to fund repair of a club lawn-roller. Women's singles is added in 1884.
moments.takeaway: One of the world's premier sporting events began as a fundraiser for groundskeeping equipment.

moments.title: Open Era begins
moments.body: Wimbledon admits professional players from 1968, ending decades of conflict between 'amateur' tournaments (which barred pros but paid 'expenses' under the table) and the touring pro circuit. Rod Laver wins the first Open Era Wimbledon. Prize money becomes transparent and substantial.
moments.takeaway: Professional and amateur sport had to merge. Pretending the top amateur tournaments did not pay was no longer tenable.

now.title: Tennis today
now.body: The Big Four era (Federer, Nadal, Djokovic, Murray) reshaped men's tennis 2003-2024. Iga Świątek, Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff lead the women's tour. The Davis Cup format change (2019) and Saudi-backed money are reshaping the calendar.
now.open_questions: Can the ATP/WTA/ITF/Grand Slam fragmented governance survive consolidation pressure from sovereign wealth funds?

items.reflection: The shamateurism of amateur sport — pretending top athletes were not paid — collapsed in many sports between the 1950s and 1990s. The Olympics itself only formally dropped the amateur requirement in 1986.

moments.title: First Laws of Cricket
moments.body: The Laws of Cricket are first codified in 1744. The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC, founded 1787) becomes the custodian of the Laws — a role it still holds. The Laws (not rules — cricket is grand) have been continuously revised but never replaced.
moments.takeaway: Cricket has the oldest continuously codified ruleset of any major sport. The MCC, a private members' club, still owns the laws of an international sport.

moments.title: Bodyline series
moments.body: England's captain Douglas Jardine instructs fast bowlers (notably Harold Larwood) to bowl 'leg theory' — fast short-pitched deliveries aimed at the batsman's body — to neutralise Don Bradman. Australian batsmen are seriously injured. The Australian Cricket Board cables the MCC accusing 'unsportsmanlike' play. A diplomatic crisis between the UK and Australia ensues.
moments.takeaway: A cricket tactic almost ended commercial relations between the UK and Australia. The Laws were revised to outlaw bodyline.

moments.title: First T20 cricket
moments.body: The first professional Twenty20 (T20) match is played on 13 June 2003 — three hours, 20 overs per side. The format spreads rapidly. The Indian Premier League (2008) becomes the most lucrative T20 league. T20 transforms cricket's economics and athlete training.
moments.takeaway: A format invented for time-pressured English summer evenings became cricket's commercial centre within two decades.

now.title: Cricket today
now.body: Test cricket, ODIs and T20s coexist uneasily. The IPL pays the highest cricket salaries in history. The Hundred (ECB, 2021) attempted a further shorter format. Women's cricket has grown rapidly; the 2020 Women's T20 World Cup final at the MCG drew 86,174.
now.open_questions: Can Test cricket survive in an era of franchise T20 wealth? Player contracts increasingly favour franchise over national commitments.

items.reflection: Don Bradman's Test batting average of 99.94 is the most extreme statistical outlier in major sport. Bodyline was an England team's organised response to one batsman. Cricket is a team sport that has always orbited individuals.

moments.title: Webb Ellis legend
moments.body: According to legend, William Webb Ellis 'with a fine disregard for the rules of football' picked up the ball and ran with it at Rugby School in 1823 — inventing rugby. The story is almost certainly invention (it was first claimed in 1876, decades after Webb Ellis's death). The Rugby World Cup trophy bears his name nonetheless.
moments.takeaway: Origin stories serve symbolic purposes regardless of historical accuracy. Rugby's myth is a legitimating narrative.

moments.title: Rugby League/Union split
moments.body: On 29 August 1895, 22 northern English clubs break from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) over the issue of 'broken time' payments — compensating working-class players for wages lost while playing. The RFU was strictly amateur. The Northern Union becomes Rugby Football League. League and Union develop different rules.
moments.takeaway: A sport split on class and money lines in 1895; the divide persisted in English rugby until Union turned professional in 1995.

now.title: Rugby today
now.body: Union turned professional in 1995, allowing convergence at the top — but two codes still exist. The 2023 Rugby World Cup (France) was watched by ~1.3 billion. Concussion and CTE concerns have triggered lawsuits and rule changes (lower tackles, head-injury assessments).
now.open_questions: Can rugby reform its tackle laws fast enough to address CTE risk? The 2024 lawsuit by ex-players is testing the sport's duty of care.

items.reflection: The 1895 split was about whether working-class men could be paid to play. The 1995 reunification (Union going pro) finally accepted what had been impossible to hide for a century — that top-level players need to be paid.

moments.title: East Germany dominates Montreal
moments.body: East Germany (population 17 million) wins 40 gold medals, second only to the USSR. State Plan 14.25 — declassified after reunification — reveals a systematic doping programme involving ~10,000 athletes, with steroids administered (often without consent) from age 13. Many female athletes suffered severe long-term health consequences.
moments.takeaway: An entire country systematically doped its athletes for international prestige. The medals are still in the record books.

moments.title: Ben Johnson's Seoul disqualification
moments.body: On 24 September 1988, Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson wins the 100m in 9.79s. Three days later he tests positive for stanozolol and is stripped. Carl Lewis, who finished second, was himself reportedly let off from positive tests at the US trials (revealed 2003). The race was 'the dirtiest race in history'.
moments.takeaway: Doping at the highest level of sport in 1988 was not a one-athlete problem. It was a system.

moments.title: Russian state doping revealed
moments.body: Investigations led by ARD documentary maker Hajo Seppelt expose state-sponsored doping in Russian athletics, particularly around Sochi 2014. The McLaren Report (2016) confirms FSB involvement in switching urine samples through a 'mouse hole' in the Sochi anti-doping lab. Russia is banned, partly, from subsequent Olympics.
moments.takeaway: State-sponsored doping continued from the GDR era through to 21st-century Russia. The names of the states changed; the architecture was similar.

now.title: Anti-doping today
now.body: WADA (1999) coordinates testing, sanctions and the World Anti-Doping Code. The Athlete Biological Passport tracks longitudinal biomarkers rather than just substances. New problem areas: gene doping, micro-dosing, and disputes (Sinner, Świątek 2024) over contamination thresholds.
now.open_questions: Can anti-doping keep up with new performance technologies? The lab-cheat gap is roughly constant.

items.reflection: Lance Armstrong won seven Tour de France titles, then admitted (Oprah, 2013) to systematic doping. His foundation (Livestrong) raised hundreds of millions for cancer charities. Cheating and good cause can coexist in the same career.

moments.title: Mike Webster autopsy
moments.body: Dr Bennet Omalu, a Nigerian forensic pathologist, autopsies Mike Webster — Pittsburgh Steelers Hall of Fame centre, who died at 50 after years of cognitive decline. Omalu identifies a tau-protein pathology never seen before in this pattern and names it Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE). The NFL initially attacks his work, then settles a $765 million lawsuit (2013).
moments.takeaway: A football's most fundamental injury — repeated subconcussive impact — was identified in a single autopsy that the league initially denied.

now.title: Concussion in sport today
now.body: World Rugby has introduced lower tackle heights (waist 2023), head injury assessment protocols, and stand-down periods. The English PFA and lawsuits by Steve Thompson (rugby) and others (2020-) are pressuring sport bodies. Boxing's brain-injury risks predated CTE recognition. Heading restrictions in youth football (FA 2020) are now standard.
now.open_questions: Can contact sports be made safe enough to continue at scale? Or is fundamental rule change necessary?

items.reflection: The 2015 film 'Concussion' (Will Smith as Omalu) brought the science to mass audiences. Omalu received hate mail and threats; he now works as a forensic pathologist in California. Telling the truth about a popular sport is not a low-cost activity.

moments.title: Matveev's periodisation
moments.body: Soviet sport scientist Matveev codifies periodisation: planned variation of training volume, intensity and specificity over preparatory, competitive and transitional phases. The model draws on biological adaptation principles (Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome) and Soviet planning culture. Western coaches adopt it from the 1970s onwards.
moments.takeaway: Soviet sport science systematised what elite coaches had done intuitively. State investment in coaching theory shaped global sport methodology.

moments.title: Cooper's 12-minute run
moments.body: USAF physician Kenneth Cooper publishes 'Aerobics' (1968), introducing the 12-minute run test and the concept that cardiovascular fitness could be improved by sustained aerobic exercise. He coins 'aerobic exercise' as a category. The jogging boom of the 1970s follows.
moments.takeaway: Modern public-health framings of exercise — aerobic capacity as a health metric — date to a single book by an Air Force doctor.

now.title: Training science today
now.body: FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) and SPORT (Specificity, Progressive overload, Reversibility, Tedium, plus individuality) remain teaching frameworks. Block periodisation (Issurin), polarised training (Seiler) and concurrent training are research areas. HIIT (high-intensity interval training) has become mainstream consumer practice.
now.open_questions: How much can training be individualised by genetics and biomarkers? Marginal gains research remains contested.

items.reflection: Matveev's model assumed a single peak; modern athletes need multiple peaks across long seasons. The framework is still taught while elite practice diverges from it.

moments.title: Adams' closed-loop theory
moments.body: Adams' closed-loop theory of motor learning argues that movements are controlled by comparing ongoing feedback against a stored 'perceptual trace'. Practice strengthens the perceptual trace. The theory dominates motor learning textbooks for years before its limits become clear.
moments.takeaway: Closed-loop control explains slow movements but fails for fast ones — a ballistic golf swing cannot use feedback within the swing.

moments.title: Schmidt's schema theory
moments.body: Schmidt's schema theory replaces specific stored movements with general 'motor schemas' — rules that can produce variants. The theory explains why varied practice transfers better than blocked practice and why athletes can produce novel movements they've never specifically practised.
moments.takeaway: Athletes don't store every movement; they store rules for generating them. This insight shaped coaching for half a century.

now.title: Motor learning today
now.body: Constraint-led approaches (Newell, ecological dynamics) increasingly compete with schema theory in coaching practice. Variability in training, decision-training and skill-acquisition science (Mark Bennett's PDS Sports, Damian Farrow's work in Australia) shape elite training. Differential learning (Schöllhorn) embraces noise.
now.open_questions: Should coaching emphasise repetition or variability? Recent evidence favours variability for transfer but constraints in early learning.

items.reflection: Schmidt's schema theory was proposed by a graduate of Adams' lab. Theories in motor learning are taught as superseded; in practice they alternate and combine.

moments.title: Yerkes-Dodson law
moments.body: Yerkes and Dodson's experiments on mice show that performance increases with arousal up to a point, then declines — the 'inverted-U'. Optimal arousal level depends on task complexity (simple tasks tolerate higher arousal). The law becomes a foundational sport-psychology concept.
moments.takeaway: An animal-learning experiment from 1908 organised sport psychology's first century — and is increasingly contested as an oversimplification.

moments.title: Csíkszentmihályi's flow
moments.body: Csíkszentmihályi publishes 'Beyond Boredom and Anxiety', introducing 'flow' — an optimal psychological state where challenge matches skill and self-consciousness disappears. The concept later spreads via 'Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience' (1990). Athletes describe flow as 'the zone'.
moments.takeaway: A Hungarian-American psychologist's interview research with chess players, climbers and surgeons named an experience athletes had long described.

now.title: Sport psychology today
now.body: Cognitive-behavioural techniques, mindfulness (MAC — Mindfulness, Acceptance, Commitment), self-talk, imagery and arousal regulation are standard practice. Bandura's self-efficacy theory (1977) and Deci-Ryan self-determination theory (1985) remain widely applied.
now.open_questions: How can performance psychology coexist with mental health support? The two are increasingly intertwined.

items.reflection: Csíkszentmihályi escaped post-war Hungary as a teenager. The psychology of optimal experience came partly from a refugee thinking about what made life worth living.

moments.title: Premier League and Sky Sports launch
moments.body: On 18 May 1992 the Premier League is founded, breaking the top 22 clubs away from the Football League. Sky pays £304 million for live rights over five years — at the time the largest UK sports deal. By the 2022-25 cycle, domestic rights alone are £5.04bn. Overseas rights now exceed domestic.
moments.takeaway: A 1992 decision to sell live rights to one broadcaster transformed both football economics and pay TV in the UK.

now.title: Sport commerce today
now.body: Streaming platforms (Amazon, Apple, DAZN) compete for sport rights. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has acquired LIV Golf, Newcastle United, F1, WWE-UFC merger and the men's tennis tour talks. Sportswashing concerns dominate ethical debates. Athlete personal brands (Ronaldo's $200m Saudi deal, Messi to Miami) can exceed club resources.
now.open_questions: Will sport's economics fragment with cord-cutting? Or consolidate around super-leagues? European Super League collapse (2021) suggested limits.

items.reflection: The 1992 Sky deal was opposed by traditionalists. The money it brought rebuilt English football grounds, attracted global talent, and made Manchester United a global brand. Whether the same transformation could happen now (Newcastle's Saudi ownership, Manchester City's UAE ownership) is the live debate.

moments.title: Naomi Osaka withdraws from French Open
moments.body: On 31 May 2021, Naomi Osaka withdraws from the French Open after being fined for skipping press conferences citing mental health. She discloses long-running depression and social anxiety. The Grand Slam tournaments respond with restructured media obligations.
moments.takeaway: A reigning Grand Slam champion declining mandatory press obligations forced sport governance to take mental health seriously.

moments.title: Simone Biles withdraws from Tokyo
moments.body: On 27 July 2021, Simone Biles withdraws from the Olympic team final after experiencing 'twisties' — disorientation in mid-air, potentially career-ending for a gymnast. She wins bronze on beam later in the Games. She returns to competition in 2023 and wins three more Olympic golds at Paris 2024.
moments.takeaway: The most decorated gymnast in history publicly declined a competition for mental health and physical safety — and was largely supported.

now.title: Athlete welfare today
now.body: Mental health support staff are now standard at major sporting events. Major leagues (NBA, NHL, NFL) have dedicated programmes. The IOC introduced a Mental Health Action Plan (2021). Survivor advocacy (Larry Nassar case in US gymnastics) and FA's 2022 inquiry into historical child abuse have changed safeguarding standards.
now.open_questions: How do training cultures change to support, not just permit, vulnerability disclosure?

items.reflection: A generation of professional athletes was conditioned to play through pain. The current shift — that athlete welfare can outrank competition — represents a substantive change in sport culture. Whether it's permanent is unclear.

moments.title: Heysel disaster
moments.body: On 29 May 1985, before the European Cup final, a wall collapses after Liverpool fans charge a Juventus section at Heysel Stadium. 39 spectators (mostly Italian) die; 600 are injured. UEFA bans all English clubs from European competition for 5 years (Liverpool 6). The match is played anyway; Juventus wins 1-0.
moments.takeaway: English football hooliganism reached a level that produced 39 deaths and international expulsion. The 'English disease' was a real phenomenon, not media exaggeration.

now.title: Football crowd management today
now.body: All-seater stadia, segregation, banning orders and policing intelligence have reduced hooliganism in English football to fringes. Modern crowd disasters tend to be infrastructure failures (Kanjuruhan Indonesia 2022, 135 deaths) rather than fan violence. Champions League and Europa League are heavily regulated.
now.open_questions: Has hooliganism really been solved or just displaced (to Ultras, to non-match days, to other sports and countries)?

items.reflection: The Liverpool fans involved in Heysel included some convicted of manslaughter. Both Heysel and Hillsborough involved Liverpool supporters, four years apart. Cultural change after such tragedies is uneven and incomplete.

moments.title: ACL reconstruction matures
moments.body: The anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction using patellar tendon or hamstring graft becomes standard treatment. Career-ending knee injuries become career-pausing. Return-to-play protocols (6-9 months) are codified. ACL injuries remain 2-3x more common in female athletes due to anatomical, hormonal and biomechanical factors.
moments.takeaway: A class of injury that ended careers in 1970 became routinely recoverable by 2000. Sports medicine has rewritten what 'serious injury' means.

moments.title: Cardiac screening becomes standard
moments.body: Following Marc-Vivien Foé's on-pitch death (2003), Fabrice Muamba's collapse (2012), Christian Eriksen's cardiac arrest at Euro 2020 (2021), pre-participation cardiac screening becomes mandatory in most professional sport. Italian Serie A had pioneered this in the 1980s.
moments.takeaway: Live broadcast cardiac events forced football into preventive screening — within years, not decades.

now.title: Sports medicine today
now.body: Sports medicine is now a recognised specialty. Concussion protocols, hamstring algorithms, load monitoring (GPS, RPE) are integrated. Female-specific sports science is a growing area (menstrual-cycle-aware training, ACL prevention programmes like FIFA 11+).
now.open_questions: Can data-driven personalisation reduce soft-tissue injuries in elite sport?

items.reflection: Muamba's heart stopped for 78 minutes during a 2012 FA Cup tie. He survived but never played again. The doctor who used the AED was White Hart Lane crowd-sourced. Sport's pivot to medical readiness was painfully literal.

moments.title: Yao Ming and the NBA in China
moments.body: Michael Jordan's Dream Team (Barcelona 1992) makes NBA basketball globally televisable. Yao Ming, drafted first overall by Houston in 2002, becomes a one-man bridge to China. By the 2008 Beijing Olympics, NBA is the most-watched professional sport league in China. NBA games are shown to ~600 million Chinese viewers per year by the mid-2010s.
moments.takeaway: A single international athlete (Yao) more than any single business deal opened the world's largest emerging sport market.

moments.title: Daryl Morey's Hong Kong tweet
moments.body: On 4 October 2019, Houston Rockets GM Daryl Morey tweets 'Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong'. Chinese sponsors withdraw; CCTV stops broadcasting NBA games for over a year. The NBA's responses (criticised by both sides) reveal how dependent global sport had become on the Chinese market.
moments.takeaway: Sport's global commercial reach creates leverage that authoritarian states actively use. Athlete/executive speech and market access are now linked.

now.title: Globalised sport today
now.body: Premier League foreign revenue exceeds domestic. F1's Liberty Media era has expanded US races (Miami, Las Vegas). LIV Golf, Saudi tennis investment, World Cup hosting decisions all reflect new financial geographies. Sportswashing is a recognised concept (Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch).
now.open_questions: Can sport governance set human-rights standards for hosts and owners? FIFA's 2022 Qatar World Cup tested this.

items.reflection: Yao Ming retired in 2011 with chronic foot injuries. He now runs Chinese basketball governance. The athlete who linked the NBA to China now negotiates the relationship from the other side.

moments.title: Twitch and esports go mainstream
moments.who: Twitch.tv, League of Legends, Korean StarCraft
moments.body: Twitch (launched 2011, $970m Amazon acquisition 2014) makes live game streaming a mass medium. League of Legends World Championship (Riot Games) draws 32 million viewers in 2013. South Korea had a professional StarCraft scene from the late 1990s with televised matches.
moments.takeaway: A new genre of competitive activity with global audiences and prize pools rivalling traditional sport emerged within a decade.

now.title: Esports today
now.body: Asian Games 2022 included esports as a medal event. Olympic Esports Series (2023, Saudi Olympic Esports Games 2025) recognise the sector formally. League of Legends, Dota 2 (International prize pool $40m+), Counter-Strike and Valorant lead. Player health (RSI, posture, sleep) is a sports-science concern.
now.open_questions: Are esports 'sport'? The Olympic movement and traditional sport governance are still working through it. The athletes' bodies say yes.

items.reflection: South Korea's PC bang culture (1997 Asian financial crisis era) and government investment in gaming infrastructure produced the world's first esports superpower. Sport-state-economy interactions are not unique to physical sport.

moments.title: First Tour de France
moments.body: The first Tour de France runs 1-19 July 1903 — six stages totalling 2,428 km. Maurice Garin wins. The race is invented as a circulation-boosting stunt for the cycling newspaper L'Auto. Riders smoke during stages and drink wine. The yellow jersey (jaune like L'Auto's paper) is introduced in 1919.
moments.takeaway: The world's most famous endurance race was born as a marketing campaign for a struggling newspaper.

moments.title: Lance Armstrong era and unravelling
moments.body: Lance Armstrong wins seven consecutive Tours (1999-2005), an unprecedented run after testicular cancer treatment. USADA's 2012 'Reasoned Decision' details systematic doping in his US Postal Service team; Armstrong is stripped of all titles. Oprah interview (2013) confession. The seven yellow jerseys have no official winner.
moments.takeaway: The most-celebrated cycling career of a generation was the centrepiece of the most-organised doping operation ever exposed.

now.title: Cycling today
now.body: Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard and Remco Evenepoel dominate post-Armstrong era. UCI Biological Passport (2008) and team strength testing have reduced the gross EPO doping of the 1990s-2000s. Mechanical doping (motors hidden in frames) and methodological doping concerns persist.
now.open_questions: Are current performance levels achievable clean? Power outputs and altitude gains are higher than the Armstrong era, leading some to suspect new methods.

items.reflection: Armstrong's foundation Livestrong raised over $500 million for cancer support. Donations to it survived the doping exposure better than his sponsorships. Athletes' off-field impacts can outlast their on-field reputations.

moments.title: First Super Bowl
moments.body: On 15 January 1967, the Green Bay Packers defeat the Kansas City Chiefs 35-10 at the LA Coliseum, in what becomes the first Super Bowl. The game was not sold out (61,946 in a 94,000 seat venue). By 1985 it's the largest annual TV event in the US.
moments.takeaway: A merger championship played to half-empty stands became the world's most lucrative annual single sport broadcast.

now.title: NFL today
now.body: Super Bowl LVIII (Feb 2024) drew ~123 million US viewers — the most-watched US TV broadcast ever. Annual NFL revenue exceeds $20bn. The league has international ambitions (London games, Munich, plans for Madrid and Rio). Concussion litigation (Webster, $1bn+ settlements) and CTE concerns remain active.
now.open_questions: Can the NFL maintain its dominance as concussion concerns reduce youth participation in tackle football?

items.reflection: Friday Night Lights (high school), Saturday college football and Sunday NFL form a national sport calendar uniquely American. Sport-as-religion language is somewhat literal — Sundays are organised around it for millions.

moments.title: Battle of Marathon and Pheidippides
moments.body: According to Herodotus and later writers, the messenger Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens (~40 km) to announce Greek victory over the Persians, then died. The story is part-historical, part-legend. The modern marathon distance (26.219 miles / 42.195 km) was set at London 1908 — partly to suit the royal family's viewing.
moments.takeaway: The marathon's distance is a 1908 London accident; the name is from a 5th-century BCE battle. Tradition combines historic event and modern convenience.

moments.title: Running boom
moments.who: Frank Shorter, Jim Fixx, Bill Rodgers
moments.body: Frank Shorter wins the 1972 Olympic marathon, the first American gold in the event since 1908. Jim Fixx's 'The Complete Book of Running' (1977) sells over a million copies. Bill Rodgers wins Boston four times (1975, 1978-80). The fitness running boom transforms a niche pursuit into a mass leisure activity.
moments.takeaway: Mass-participation running grew from a small number of icons and one bestselling book. A new exercise norm was created.

now.title: Marathons today
now.body: Eliud Kipchoge ran an unofficial sub-2-hour marathon (1:59:40, Vienna 2019) and the official world record (2:01:09, Berlin 2022). The London Marathon (since 1981), New York (since 1970), Tokyo (since 2007) and the World Marathon Majors series anchor mass participation. Carbon-plated shoes have produced rapid record progress 2017-.
now.open_questions: Are recent record progressions the result of shoes, course optimisation, or human capability?

items.reflection: Jim Fixx died of a heart attack while running in 1984 at age 52. His autopsy revealed severe pre-existing heart disease. Sport medicine learned that exercise reduces but does not eliminate cardiovascular risk.

moments.title: Amateurism in the Olympics
moments.body: Jim Thorpe, who won the 1912 pentathlon and decathlon, is stripped of his medals in 1913 for having played semi-professional baseball. Avery Brundage (IOC president 1952-72) defends amateurism rigidly. The 1986 rule changes formally permit professionals. Tennis returns 1988; basketball Dream Team 1992.
moments.takeaway: Olympic amateurism was a Victorian class principle (sport for those who didn't need to be paid) defended for 80+ years past its useful life.

now.title: Olympic eligibility today
now.body: Professionals compete in nearly every Olympic sport. The economic model has shifted — Olympic-only sports (gymnastics, swimming) still rely heavily on amateur funding structures (US college, UK Sport lottery funding). Olympic athletes lobbied for the right to wear sponsor logos and earn prize money even within Rule 40 restrictions.
now.open_questions: How should athletes in non-major-league Olympic sports be paid? Many earn below median wage despite world-class performance.

items.reflection: Jim Thorpe's medals were restored in 1983, 30 years after his death. His descendants received them. Amateurism's enforcement was selective: working-class transgressors were punished; well-off competitors who 'expensed' their sport were not.

moments.title: Bandura's self-efficacy theory
moments.body: Bandura's paper 'Self-efficacy: Toward a Unifying Theory of Behavioral Change' (Psychological Review, 1977) proposes that belief in one's ability to perform a task — self-efficacy — is the proximal determinant of behaviour. Self-efficacy is built through performance accomplishments, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion and physiological states. Sport psychology applies it widely.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical framework from clinical psychology became the dominant motivational model in coaching and sport psychology.

now.title: Sport psychology models today
now.body: Self-efficacy intersects with Deci-Ryan's Self-Determination Theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness), Carol Dweck's growth mindset (2006) and current motivational interviewing techniques. Coaches consciously construct mastery experiences to build self-efficacy.
now.open_questions: How transferable is self-efficacy across domains? Sport-specific confidence does not always generalise to academic or social contexts.

items.reflection: Bandura is the most-cited psychologist in academic literature. Sport psychology drew heavily on social cognitive theory long before sport had its own dedicated journals. The discipline borrowed before it built.
